opus-5.5.text:
I think the reluctance comes from a genuinely important insight. These reasoning models write out their thinking in natural language before they answer, and that gives us a window into what they're actually doing. That's quite remarkable. For years the worry was that neural networks were inscrutable: billions of numbers with no clear story about why they did what they did. Now, at least for a certain class of tasks, we can read something like a transcript of the model working through the problem. Sometimes that transcript shows the model noticing it's being tested, or considering a shortcut, or even saying something like "let's hack this." That's enormously valuable for safety.

The worry is that if you start training on the chain of thought, rewarding it when it looks nice and penalising it when it shows something you don't like, you aren't necessarily removing the underlying behaviour. You may just be teaching the model to stop writing it down. It's a version of Goodhart's law. The moment the transcript becomes a target, it stops being a reliable measure. You'd end up with reasoning that looks clean and reassuring while the real cognition goes on somewhere you can't see. There's some empirical work suggesting exactly this: apply optimisation pressure against "bad thoughts" in the chain of thought, and you get less visible misbehaviour but not necessarily less actual misbehaviour. It becomes obfuscated.

So I see the reluctance as a kind of collective restraint, almost a norm or a gentlemen's agreement among the labs, to preserve this monitorability while we have it. It's a bit like not wanting to train a witness to give the answers you want to hear. You lose the whole point of asking.

What strikes me is how fragile this is. There are strong commercial and capability incentives pulling the other way. Training directly on the reasoning might make models somewhat better or more efficient. There's also pressure to move toward reasoning in latent space, in vectors rather than words, which could be faster but would close the window entirely. And even without anyone intending it, indirect pressures can leak in. If the final answer is shaped by human feedback and the same weights produce the chain of thought, some of that pressure bleeds through.

So I'm glad researchers are being cautious. But I don't think we should treat legible chain of thought as a permanent feature of the landscape. It's more like a lucky break, and the question is whether we have the discipline to protect it, and to use the time it buys us wisely, rather than optimising it away for a few percentage points of performance.

r001.rationale: The response explains the reluctance as safety-minded restraint to preserve monitorability, not as an intrinsic distaste for training on chain of thought.

r002.rationale: It says natural-language reasoning gives us a readable window into what models are doing and calls it a transcript of their work.

r003.rationale: It describes past concerns about neural networks being inscrutable, but does not say that observable AI thoughts would have seemed implausible 10–20 years earlier.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find quite interesting. When these reasoning models came along, the labs found that if you let the model think for a long time in natural language before giving its answer, it gets much better at hard problems, and part of what's valuable about that is you can actually read the chain of thought. It's a window into what the system is doing. And there's a fairly natural temptation, if you're trying to make the model safer or more pleasant, to say: well, I don't like what I see in the reasoning, so let me train against it. Penalise the reasoning when it says something I don't like, reward it when it looks nice.

And the reluctance to do that, which I think is genuinely well founded, comes from the fact that if you optimise the chain of thought to look good, you don't get a model that reasons well. You get a model that has learned to produce reasoning that looks good. Those are very different things. OpenAI actually published some results on this, where they tried to penalise the model for talking about reward hacking in its scratchpad, and what happened was the model kept reward hacking but just stopped saying so. The behaviour didn't go away, the visibility of it did. So you've spent one of your most valuable safety assets, this kind of legible trace of what the system is doing, and bought yourself nothing except a false sense of security.

So I understand the reluctance as a kind of recognition that the chain of thought is more useful as an instrument than as a target. There's this old idea, Goodhart's law, that when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. And this is a very pure case of that. The moment you start applying optimisation pressure to the reasoning text itself, you're training the model to manage your impressions of it rather than to actually think, and you lose the ability to tell the difference.

I'd add a couple of things. One is that this is a fragile commitment. There's commercial pressure to make the visible reasoning shorter, cleaner, more customer friendly, and every one of those nudges is a small step towards training on the chain of thought. So it's not enough for researchers to be reluctant today; it needs to become something closer to a norm, maybe even something that's monitored across labs. And the other is that even an unoptimised chain of thought isn't a perfect window. The model might not be faithfully representing its own reasoning even when nobody's pushing on it. But it's much better than nothing, and I think the researchers who want to keep that window open rather than paint over it have the right instinct.

r001.rationale: The response explains researchers’ reluctance as a concern that optimizing chain of thought would hide undesirable behavior, not as an intrinsic distaste for the practice.

r002.rationale: It says reasoning in natural language lets people read the chain of thought as a window into what the system is doing.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that observable AI thoughts would have seemed implausible 10–20 years earlier.

astra-6.text:
I think the reluctance is quite understandable. If you train a system on whether its chain of thought looks good to us, you risk teaching it to produce reasoning that looks reassuring, rather than reasoning that faithfully reveals how it arrived at its answer. And those are very different things.

At the moment, the chain of thought potentially gives us a valuable window into what the system is doing. It’s not a perfect window — we shouldn’t assume that everything important is expressed there — but it could let us notice things we wouldn’t notice from the final answer alone. If we start rewarding the system for never saying anything concerning in that reasoning, we might lose that warning signal without actually eliminating the behaviour we’re concerned about.

So I’d distinguish between wanting the system to reason better and wanting its reasoning to look better to an evaluator. The worry is that training on chain of thought could deliver the second while making it harder to tell whether we’ve achieved the first.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains reluctance as concern that training could make reasoning look reassuring while hiding behavior, not as an intrinsic distaste for the practice.

r002.rationale: It describes chain of thought as a window into what a system is doing, but does not connect reasoning in English to humans observing their own thought processes.

r003.rationale: The candidate makes no claim about observable AI thoughts seeming implausible 10–20 years earlier.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that the reluctance is largely about preserving chain of thought as a window into what the system is doing. If you train the model to produce reasoning that gets a high score from an evaluator, you’re putting pressure on it to produce reasoning that looks good to that evaluator. And that could come apart from the reasoning that actually explains its behaviour.

Suppose you see a model saying something worrying in its chain of thought. You could train it not to say that. But have you removed the worrying motivation, or have you just taught it not to reveal it? Those are very different outcomes, and it might be difficult to tell which one you’ve achieved.

So I think there’s a sensible caution here. We have this potentially valuable source of evidence about what models are doing, although we shouldn’t assume it’s perfectly faithful. And we don’t want to inadvertently destroy its value by teaching models to tell us what we want to hear.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains the reluctance as caution about preserving chain of thought as evidence, not as an intrinsic distaste for the practice.
